claim: DMRT1 is the testis-determining factor in several species of vertebrates.
source: DMRT1 is the testis-determining factor in several species of vertebrates, but its involvement in mammalian testes differentiation, where SRY is the testis-determining gene, remains ambiguous.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on DMRT1 function in vertebrates, as indicated in the introduction section.

claim: SRY is the testis-determining gene in mammals.
source: DMRT1 is the testis-determining factor in several species of vertebrates, but its involvement in mammalian testes differentiation, where SRY is the testis-determining gene, remains ambiguous.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian sex determination.

claim: DMRT1 loss-of-function induces Disorders of Sex Development (46, XY DSD) in men.
source: So far, DMRT1 loss-of-function has been described in two mammalian species and induces different phenotypes: Disorders of Sex Development (46, XY DSD) in men and male infertility in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on human DMRT1 mutations.

claim: DMRT1 loss-of-function induces male infertility in mice.
source: So far, DMRT1 loss-of-function has been described in two mammalian species and induces different phenotypes: Disorders of Sex Development (46, XY DSD) in men and male infertility in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on mouse Dmrt1 knockout.

claim: Gonads from XY DMRT1−/− rabbit fetuses differentiated like ovaries.
source: First, we observed that gonads from XY DMRT1−/− rabbit fetuses differentiated like ovaries, highlighting that DMRT1 is involved in testis determination.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the DMRT1 knockout rabbit model presented in the manuscript.

claim: DMRT1 is involved in testis determination in rabbits.
source: First, we observed that gonads from XY DMRT1−/− rabbit fetuses differentiated like ovaries, highlighting that DMRT1 is involved in testis determination.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that XY DMRT1−/− gonads differentiate as ovaries.

claim: DMRT1 is required in the supporting cells to increase the expression of the SOX9 gene.
source: In addition to SRY, DMRT1 is required in the supporting cells to increase the expression of the SOX9 gene, which heads the testicular genetic cascade.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced SOX9 expression in DMRT1−/− gonads.

claim: SOX9 heads the testicular genetic cascade.
source: In addition to SRY, DMRT1 is required in the supporting cells to increase the expression of the SOX9 gene, which heads the testicular genetic cascade.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SOX9's role in testis development.

claim: XX and XY DMRT1−/− ovaries did not undergo meiosis and folliculogenesis.
source: Second, we highlighted another function of DMRT1 in the germline since XX and XY DMRT1−/− ovaries did not undergo meiosis and folliculogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and molecular data presented in the manuscript.

claim: XX DMRT1−/− adult females were sterile.
source: XX DMRT1−/− adult females were sterile, showing that DMRT1 is also crucial for female fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of adult DMRT1−/− females.

claim: DMRT1 is crucial for female fertility.
source: XX DMRT1−/− adult females were sterile, showing that DMRT1 is also crucial for female fertility.
evidence: This is inferred from the sterility observed in XX DMRT1−/− females.

claim: There is an evolutionary continuum between non-mammalian vertebrates such as birds and non-rodent mammals regarding DMRT1 function.
source: To conclude, these phenotypes indicate an evolutionary continuum between non-mammalian vertebrates such as birds and non-rodent mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of DMRT1 phenotypes across species.

claim: DMRT1 mutations may be involved in 46, XY DSD in humans.
source: Furthermore, our data support the potential involvement of DMRT1 mutations in different human pathologies, such as 46, XY DSD as well as male and female infertility.
evidence: This is speculative based on the rabbit data and prior human case reports.

claim: DMRT1 mutations may be involved in male and female infertility in humans.
source: Furthermore, our data support the potential involvement of DMRT1 mutations in different human pathologies, such as 46, XY DSD as well as male and female infertility.
evidence: This is speculative based on the rabbit data and prior human case reports.

claim: DMRT1 belongs to the highly conserved family of DM domain proteins.
source: DMRT1 (Doublesex and Mab-3 Related Transcription factor 1) belongs to the highly conserved family of DM domain proteins, which exhibits a zinc finger DNA-binding motif that was initially identified in Drosophilia and Caenorhabditis elegans (Erdman and Burtis, 1993; Raymond et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on DM domain proteins.

claim: DM domain proteins exhibit a zinc finger DNA-binding motif initially identified in Drosophila and Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: DMRT1 (Doublesex and Mab-3 Related Transcription factor 1) belongs to the highly conserved family of DM domain proteins, which exhibits a zinc finger DNA-binding motif that was initially identified in Drosophilia and Caenorhabditis elegans (Erdman and Burtis, 1993; Raymond et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: DMRT1 orthologs have been described as Testis-Determining Factor in medaka (Oryzias latipes).
source: Some of its orthologs have been described as Testis-Determining Factor (TDF) in vertebrate species such as medaka (Oryzias latipes) (Matsuda et al., 2002), xenope (Xenopus laevis) (Yoshimoto et al., 2010), or chicken (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matsuda et al., 2002.

claim: DMRT1 orthologs have been described as Testis-Determining Factor in xenope (Xenopus laevis).
source: Some of its orthologs have been described as Testis-Determining Factor (TDF) in vertebrate species such as medaka (Oryzias latipes) (Matsuda et al., 2002), xenope (Xenopus laevis) (Yoshimoto et al., 2010), or chicken (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yoshimoto et al., 2010.

claim: DMRT1 orthologs have been described as Testis-Determining Factor in chicken.
source: Some of its orthologs have been described as Testis-Determining Factor (TDF) in vertebrate species such as medaka (Oryzias latipes) (Matsuda et al., 2002), xenope (Xenopus laevis) (Yoshimoto et al., 2010), or chicken (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2009.

claim: The Z chromosome carries the DMRT1 gene in chicken.
source: In the last, the Z chromosome carries the DMRT1 gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chicken sex determination.

claim: In ZZ male chickens, two copies of the DMRT1 gene are required to induce testis determination.
source: In ZZ males, two copies of the DMRT1 gene are required to induce testis determination.
evidence: This is supported by citation to research on chicken sex determination.

claim: In ZW female chickens and ZZ chickens harboring a non-functional copy, gonads differentiate as ovaries.
source: In ZW females and ZZ chickens harboring a non-functional copy, gonads differentiate as ovaries showing that sex determination is based on DMRT1 dosage (Ioannidis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ioannidis et al., 2021.

claim: Sex determination in chicken is based on DMRT1 dosage.
source: In ZW females and ZZ chickens harboring a non-functional copy, gonads differentiate as ovaries showing that sex determination is based on DMRT1 dosage (Ioannidis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ioannidis et al., 2021.

claim: The sex-determining system in mammals is XX/XY.
source: In mammals, where the sex-determining system is XX/XY, the TDF is the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region of the Y chromosome) carried by the Y chromosome.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian sex determination.

claim: The TDF in mammals is the SRY gene carried by the Y chromosome.
source: In mammals, where the sex-determining system is XX/XY, the TDF is the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region of the Y chromosome) carried by the Y chromosome.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian sex determination.

claim: DMRT1 does not appear to have retained a crucial function in testis determination in mice.
source: Based on the mouse species, DMRT1 does not appear to have retained a crucial function in testis determination since targeted deletion of Dmrt1 only affects post-natal testis function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior mouse research.

claim: Targeted deletion of Dmrt1 in mice only affects post-natal testis function.
source: Based on the mouse species, DMRT1 does not appear to have retained a crucial function in testis determination since targeted deletion of Dmrt1 only affects post-natal testis function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior mouse research.

claim: DMRT1 has roles in both germ cells and supporting cells in the testis.
source: In fact, DMRT1 has roles in both germ cells and supporting cells in the testis, and Dmrt1−/− males showed spermatogenesis failure with spermatogonia that did not undergo meiosis (Matson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matson et al., 2010.

claim: Dmrt1−/− males showed spermatogenesis failure with spermatogonia that did not undergo meiosis.
source: In fact, DMRT1 has roles in both germ cells and supporting cells in the testis, and Dmrt1−/− males showed spermatogenesis failure with spermatogonia that did not undergo meiosis (Matson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matson et al., 2010.

claim: Specific knock-out of Dmrt1 in adult Sertoli cells led to their transdifferentiation into granulosa cells.
source: However, specific knock-out of Dmrt1 in adult Sertoli cells led to their transdifferentiation into granulosa cells (Matson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matson et al., 2011.

claim: DMRT1 is necessary to maintain Sertoli cell identity in adulthood in mice.
source: Although DMRT1 is not required for testis determination in mice, it retained part of its function in adulthood when it is necessary to maintain Sertoli cell identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the transdifferentiation observed in Dmrt1 knockout Sertoli cells.

claim: In mice, Foxl2 is expressed in female-supporting cells early in development but does not appear necessary for fetal ovary differentiation.
source: In the mouse, Foxl2 is expressed in female-supporting cells early in development but does not appear necessary for fetal ovary differentiation (Uda et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Uda et al., 2004.

claim: FOXL2 is required in adult granulosa cells to maintain female-supporting cell identity in mice.
source: On the contrary, it is required in adult granulosa cells to maintain female-supporting cell identity (Ottolenghi et al., 2005; Uhlenhaut et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ottolenghi et al., 2005 and Uhlenhaut et al., 2009.

claim: FOXL2 is crucial for ovarian determination in goats.
source: In other mammalian species, such as goats, FOXL2 was shown to be crucial for ovarian determination.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to goat research.

claim: FOXL2 loss-of-function led to female-to-male sex reversal with the early development of XX testes in goats.
source: Indeed, naturally observed in the PIS (Polled Intersex Syndrome) mutation (Pailhoux et al., 2001) or experimentally induced by genome editing in goats (Boulanger et al., 2014), FOXL2 loss-of-function led to female-to-male sex reversal with the early development of XX testes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pailhoux et al., 2001 and Boulanger et al., 2014.

claim: Following FOXL2 absence of expression in XX mutant goat gonads, DMRT1 was up-regulated within days before increased SOX9 expression.
source: Following FOXL2 absence of expression in the XX mutant gonads (XX PIS−/− or XX FOXL2−/−), DMRT1 was up-regulated within days before increased SOX9 expression, which then directs the differentiation of Sertoli cells and the formation of testicular cords (Elzaiat et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Elzaiat et al., 2014.

claim: DMRT1 could retain function in SOX9 activation and testis determination in several mammals.
source: These observations in the goat suggested that DMRT1 could retain function in SOX9 activation and, thus, in testis determination in several mammals.
evidence: This is speculative based on goat data.

claim: A few mutations affecting DMRT1 have been described in patients presenting 46, XY DSD.
source: In humans, a few mutations affecting DMRT1 have been described in patients presenting 46, XY DSD (Disorders of Sex Development) (Chauhan et al., 2017; Ledig et al., 2012; Mello et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chauhan et al., 2017; Ledig et al., 2012; Mello et al., 2010.

claim: A heterozygous de novo point mutation in the DMRT1 gene has been identified in a 46, XY individual with complete gonadal dysgenesis.
source: In particular, a heterozygous de novo point mutation in the DMRT1 gene has been identified in a 46, XY individual with complete gonadal dysgenesis (Murphy et al., 2015), suggesting that DMRT1 and SRY may be involved in testicular determination.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Murphy et al., 2015.

claim: DMRT1 and SRY may be involved in testicular determination in humans.
source: In particular, a heterozygous de novo point mutation in the DMRT1 gene has been identified in a 46, XY individual with complete gonadal dysgenesis (Murphy et al., 2015), suggesting that DMRT1 and SRY may be involved in testicular determination.
evidence: This is speculative based on the human case report.

claim: A DMRT1 mutant rabbit line was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
source: To clarify DMRT1 functions in non-rodent mammals, we have chosen the rabbit model, where we generated a DMRT1 mutant line thanks to the CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Both XY and XX fetal rabbit gonads expressed DMRT1 before their sexual differentiation.
source: Firstly, we characterized the DMRT1 expression in control gonads, showing that both XY and XX fetal gonads were expressing DMRT1 before their sexual differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: In XY rabbit fetuses, DMRT1 and SRY presented partially overlapping territory.
source: In XY fetuses, DMRT1 and SRY presented partially overlapping territory, and somatic cells expressing both of them harbored SOX9 expression and differentiated into Sertoli cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Somatic cells expressing both DMRT1 and SRY harbored SOX9 expression and differentiated into Sertoli cells in rabbit fetuses.
source: In XY fetuses, DMRT1 and SRY presented partially overlapping territory, and somatic cells expressing both of them harbored SOX9 expression and differentiated into Sertoli cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: DMRT1 was required for testis differentiation in rabbits since XY DMRT1−/− rabbits showed early male-to-female sex reversal with differentiating ovaries and complete female genitalia.
source: Secondly, thanks to our CRISPR/Cas9 genetically modified rabbit model, we demonstrated that DMRT1 was required for testis differentiation since XY DMRT1−/− rabbits showed early male-to-female sex reversal with differentiating ovaries and complete female genitalia.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and molecular data from DMRT1−/− rabbits.

claim: Germ cells failed to undergo meiosis in XY and XX DMRT1−/− mutant ovaries.
source: However, germ cells failed to undergo meiosis, and follicles did not form in XY and XX DMRT1−/− mutant ovaries, leading to female infertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data from DMRT1−/− ovaries.

claim: Follicles did not form in XY and XX DMRT1−/− mutant ovaries.
source: However, germ cells failed to undergo meiosis, and follicles did not form in XY and XX DMRT1−/− mutant ovaries, leading to female infertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data from DMRT1−/− ovaries.

claim: DMRT1 is a testis-determining factor in mammals.
source: Finally, we demonstrated that DMRT1 was a testis-determining factor in mammals and that it was also required for female fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the rabbit model.

claim: DMRT1 is required for female fertility in mammals.
source: Finally, we demonstrated that DMRT1 was a testis-determining factor in mammals and that it was also required for female fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the rabbit model.

claim: DMRT1 expression pattern has been reported by molecular analysis in the rabbit species from 14 dpc to adulthood.
source: DMRT1 expression pattern has already been reported by molecular analysis in the rabbit species from 14 dpc to adulthood (Daniel-Carlier et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Daniel-Carlier et al., 2013.

claim: SRY expression was detected at 12 dpc and was found only in the XY genital ridges, restricted to the medullary part of the gonad.
source: SRY expression was already detected at 12 dpc and, as expected, was found only in the XY genital ridges, where it was restricted to the medullary part of the gonad (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMRT1 was faintly expressed in the gonads of both sexes at 12 dpc, in a few cells of the medulla under the coelomic epithelium.
source: In contrast, DMRT1 was faintly expressed in the gonads of both sexes, in a few cells of the medulla under the coelomic epithelium (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 12 dpc, only very few germ cells, expressing POU5F1, have completed their migration into the genital ridges.
source: At 12 dpc, only very few germ cells, expressing POU5F1, have completed their migration into the genital ridges (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 13 dpc, the genital ridges had tripled in size in both sexes.
source: Twenty-four hours later, at 13 dpc, the genital ridges had tripled in size in both sexes, and the territory of SRY expression increased within the XY developing testes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The territory of SRY expression increased within the XY developing testes at 13 dpc.
source: Twenty-four hours later, at 13 dpc, the genital ridges had tripled in size in both sexes, and the territory of SRY expression increased within the XY developing testes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of somatic cells expressing DMRT1 was strongly increased at 13 dpc in both sexes, with few of them located in the coelomic epithelium.
source: The number of somatic cells expressing DMRT1 was also strongly increased in both sexes, with few of them located in the coelomic epithelium (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: More POU5F1-expressing germ cells were detected at 13 dpc (5–12 per section instead of 1 or 2 at 12 dpc).
source: In addition, more POU5F1-expressing germ cells were detected (5–12 per section instead of 1 or 2 at 12 dpc) (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: At 14 dpc, the SOX9 protein was immunodetected in a few cells located in the medullary part of the XY gonad.
source: At 14 dpc, the SOX9 protein was immunodetected in a few cells located in the medullary part of the XY gonad (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Numerous somatic cells in the medullary region of XY gonads at 14 dpc expressed SRY and DMRT1.
source: Numerous somatic cells of this region also expressed SRY and DMRT1 (Figure 2), and a few co-expressed SOX9 and DMRT1 simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A few cells co-expressed SOX9 and DMRT1 simultaneously at 14 dpc in XY gonads.
source: Numerous somatic cells of this region also expressed SRY and DMRT1 (Figure 2), and a few co-expressed SOX9 and DMRT1 simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Coelomic epithelial cells only expressed DMRT1 at 14 dpc in XY gonads.
source: In contrast, coelomic epithelial cells only expressed DMRT1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At 15 dpc, Sertoli cells that co-express SRY, DMRT1, and SOX9 began to be organized into embryonic cords.
source: At 15 dpc, Sertoli cells that co-express SRY, DMRT1, and SOX9 began to be organized into embryonic cords (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At 15 dpc, coelomic epithelial cells expressed DMRT1 but were negative for SRY and SOX9.
source: At this stage, coelomic epithelial cells expressed DMRT1 but were negative for SRY and SOX9.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: An islet of cells expressing SRY and DMRT1 was observed in the mesonephros below the boundary with the gonad at 15 dpc.
source: Furthermore, we observed an islet of cells expressing SRY and DMRT1 located in the mesonephros below the boundary with the gonad (Figure 2, dotted line).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The islet of cells expressing SRY and DMRT1 in the mesonephros expressed PAX8.
source: These cells expressed PAX8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and could correspond to the recently described supporting-like cell population contributing to the rete testis in mice (Mayère et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The PAX8-positive cells in the mesonephros could correspond to the recently described supporting-like cell population contributing to the rete testis in mice.
source: These cells expressed PAX8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and could correspond to the recently described supporting-like cell population contributing to the rete testis in mice (Mayère et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculative based on comparison with mouse data.

claim: PAX8-positive cells will express SOX9 at later stages in rabbit development.
source: As in mice, these cells will express SOX9 at the latter stages (a few of them are already SOX9 positive at 15 dpc), but unlike mice, they express SRY.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that a few cells are already SOX9 positive at 15 dpc.

claim: Unlike mice, PAX8-positive cells in rabbits express SRY.
source: As in mice, these cells will express SOX9 at the latter stages (a few of them are already SOX9 positive at 15 dpc), but unlike mice, they express SRY.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: From 16 to 18 dpc, the development of the testicular cords proceeded.
source: From 16 to 18 dpc, the development of the testicular cords proceeded.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations.

claim: At 16 and 18 dpc, SRY, DMRT1, and SOX9 were expressed only in the Sertoli cells.
source: At these two stages (16 and 18 dpc), SRY, DMRT1, and SOX9 were expressed only in the Sertoli cells, where SRY expression began to decrease from 18 dpc (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: SRY expression began to decrease from 18 dpc.
source: At these two stages (16 and 18 dpc), SRY, DMRT1, and SOX9 were expressed only in the Sertoli cells, where SRY expression began to decrease from 18 dpc (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: No more DMRT1 expression could be seen in the coelomic epithelial cells at 16 and 18 dpc.
source: No more DMRT1 expression could be seen in the coelomic epithelial cells, but the tunica albuginea begins to form (Figure 2), and consequently, the coelomic epithelium will become the surface epithelium.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The tunica albuginea begins to form at 16 and 18 dpc.
source: No more DMRT1 expression could be seen in the coelomic epithelial cells, but the tunica albuginea begins to form (Figure 2), and consequently, the coelomic epithelium will become the surface epithelium.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The coelomic epithelium will become the surface epithelium after tunica albuginea formation.
source: No more DMRT1 expression could be seen in the coelomic epithelial cells, but the tunica albuginea begins to form (Figure 2), and consequently, the coelomic epithelium will become the surface epithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental process.

claim: DMRT1 expression started at 12 dpc in the gonadal somatic compartment of both sexes.
source: As described above, DMRT1 expression started at 12 dpc in the gonadal somatic compartment of both sexes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the female gonads, DMRT1 remained expressed in all somatic cells, including those of the coelomic epithelium, until 16 dpc.
source: In the female gonads, DMRT1 remained expressed in all somatic cells, including those of the coelomic epithelium, until 16 dpc (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PAX8-positive cells were observed in XX gonads at 15 dpc.
source: Interestingly, as in XY gonads, we observed PAX8-positive cells in XX gonads at 15 dpc (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PAX8-positive cells in XX gonads could contribute to the formation of the rete ovarii as in mice.
source: These cells could contribute to the formation of the rete ovarii as in mice (Mayère et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculative based on comparison with mouse data.

claim: At 18 dpc, DMRT1 expression decreased but persisted in some cells located in the coelomic epithelium and just below it, where ovigerous nest formation occurred.
source: At 18 dpc, DMRT1 expression decreased but persisted in some cells located in the coelomic epithelium and just below it, where ovigerous nest formation occurred.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The female DMRT1-antagonist gene FOXL2 began to be expressed between 16 and 18 dpc when DMRT1 expression decreased.
source: Interestingly, the female DMRT1-antagonist gene FOXL2 began to be expressed between 16 and 18 dpc when DMRT1 expression decreased (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 20 dpc, DMRT1 expression was limited in some somatic cells enclosed in nascent ovigerous nests where some germinal cells also began to be positive for DMRT1.
source: Thereafter, at 20 dpc, DMRT1 expression was limited in some somatic cells enclosed in nascent ovigerous nests where some germinal cells also began to be positive for DMRT1 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 20 dpc, DMRT1-positive territory seems to overlap that of RSPO1 but not that of FOXL2 located in the loose conjunctive tissue around the ovigerous nests.
source: At this stage, DMRT1-positive territory seems to overlap that of RSPO1 but not that of FOXL2 located in the loose conjunctive tissue around the ovigerous nests (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A DMRT1 knock-out rabbit line was engineered using the CRISPR/Cas9 system with two RNA guides located in exon 3.
source: To determine the role of DMRT1 in the rabbit species used as a non-rodent mammalian model, we engineered a DMRT1 knock-out line using the CRISPR/Cas9 system with two RNA guides located in exon 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental methods described in the manuscript.

claim: The mutation carried by the DMRT1 knock-out rabbit line is a 47-bp duplication in sense, leading to a frameshift of the open reading frame and a premature stop codon.
source: The mutation carried by this line is a 47-bp duplication in sense, leading to a frameshift of the open reading frame and a premature stop codon (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The DMRT1 mutation does not affect DMRT1 transcription but induces a total absence of protein.
source: This mutation does not affect DMRT1 transcription but induces a total absence of protein as shown in post-natal gonads by western blot (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: At 20 dpc, testes appeared with well-formed seminiferous cords in control animals.
source: Indeed, at this stage, testes appeared with well-formed seminiferous cords, and ovigerous nest formation was clearly in progress in the ovaries (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ovigerous nest formation was clearly in progress in the ovaries at 20 dpc in control animals.
source: Indeed, at this stage, testes appeared with well-formed seminiferous cords, and ovigerous nest formation was clearly in progress in the ovaries (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 20 dpc, XY DMRT1−/− gonads failed to engage testicular differentiation and appeared quite like control ovaries.
source: At 20 dpc, XY DMRT1−/− gonads failed to engage testicular differentiation and appeared quite like control ovaries, but ovarian differentiation did not appear to be affected by the loss of DMRT1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ovarian differentiation did not appear to be affected by the loss of DMRT1 at 20 dpc.
source: At 20 dpc, XY DMRT1−/− gonads failed to engage testicular differentiation and appeared quite like control ovaries, but ovarian differentiation did not appear to be affected by the loss of DMRT1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 3640 genes were differentially expressed in at least one of the four genotypes (adjusted p-value <0.05 and |log2FC| > 1).
source: Heatmap representation of the 3640 differentially expressed genes in at least one of the four genotypes (adjusted p-value <0.05 and |log2FC| > 1; Supplementary file 1) was clustered into eight groups (#1 to #8, Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Clusters #1 and #7 contained 1331 and 315 genes, respectively, which were preferentially expressed in XY control testes.
source: Clusters #1 and #7 contained 1331 and 315 genes, respectively, which were preferentially expressed in XY control testes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Expression of genes in clusters #1 and #7 was decreased in XY DMRT1−/− gonads, harboring levels close to that of the female's ovaries.
source: Expression of these genes was decreased in XY DMRT1−/− gonads, harboring levels close to that of the female's ovaries (XX control or DMRT1−/−).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Clusters #2, #3, and #5 (537, 582, and 464 genes, respectively) were composed of genes preferentially expressed in XX control ovaries.
source: On the other hand, clusters #2, #3, and #5 (537, 582, and 464 genes, respectively) were composed of genes preferentially expressed in XX control ovaries, and their expression was increased in XY DMRT1−/− gonads.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis.
